strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing genuine limitations of prior work (speech generation capability and architectural complexity)
Elegant and simple joint self-attention design that effectively unifies cross-modal interaction without additional fusion modules, supported by comprehensive ablations (Table 5)
Effective mouth-area loss strategy with thorough validation through zero-masking experiments; dramatic improvement demonstrated (LSE-C 1.39→6.50)
Strong experimental results on two benchmarks with diverse evaluation metrics; particularly impressive efficiency: achieves LSE-C 6.20 with 3.2B parameters vs. Universe-1 (7.1B, LSE-C 1.62)
Comprehensive ablation studies examining mouth-loss weight λ, temporal-aligned RoPE, and fusion strategies with clear trade-off analysis
Thoughtful multi-component dataset construction (4.2M hours) with comprehensive annotation pipeline providing tri-level supervision (video, audio, speech captions)
Clear presentation with detailed diagrams, mathematical formulations, and implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: joint attention is straightforward concatenation + standard self-attention; mouth-area loss is incremental region-weighted supervision; primary contribution is system design rather than novel techniques

Missing human evaluation studies despite lip-sync and video-audio quality being inherently perceptual tasks; relies entirely on automated metrics (SyncNet 2016, WER, aesthetic scores) without inter-rater validation

Insufficient analysis of design choices: unclear why duplicating video backbone for audio initialization, how joint attention learns sparse correlations (mouth ~2.3% of frames), and inadequate exploration of temporal-aligned RoPE trade-off (FD decreases from 0.69→0.58)

Limited evaluation scope: UniAvatar-Bench contains only 100 samples; both benchmarks focus narrowly on talking head videos with unclear generalization to other human-speech scenarios (musicians, multiple speakers, non-English, extreme poses)
Incomplete dataset attribution: talking head videos from 'publicly available sources' without specific citations; unclear data provenance and copyright considerations
No failure analysis or discussion of limitations: when does mouth-area loss not help (occlusion, extreme angles, partial visibility)? No confidence intervals or error analysis provided
Fairness of comparisons: main results use 24B parameters (vs. Universe-1 7.1B, OVI 10.9B); JoVA-1.6B evaluated separately, weakening headline efficiency claims
Cross-attention comparison fairness: 'cross-attention with linear' achieving LSE-C 1.63 seems suspiciously low; implementation correctness unclear, limiting architectural superiority claims
Missing technical details: classifier-free guidance implementation, inference time/memory comparisons, how concatenation affects computational requirements vs. dual-branch approaches
Incomplete declaration section: 'will not be integrated into any products of .' appears truncated; reproducibility concern about code/model release not mentioned

strengths: Clear problem motivation and architectural visualization effectively communicating design rationale
Comprehensive quantitative evaluation across multiple metrics and two benchmarks with systematic ablation studies
Convincing mouth-region localization validation using zero-masking in VAE latent space with visual evidence
Strong empirical results across most metrics, particularly on lip-sync (LSE-C: 6.64) and speech quality (WER: 0.18)
Demonstrates efficiency with smaller models (3.2B parameters, 1.9M samples) achieving competitive performance
Good presentation quality with clear figures and organized exposition
weaknesses: Joint self-attention is a standard multimodal learning technique (e.g., BERT for multi-modal inputs), not a novel contribution; oversold as major architectural innovation
Mouth-area loss reduces to simple region-weighted MSE loss, a technique widely used in medical imaging and focal losses; limited novelty in application

Critical finding insufficiently addressed: LSE-C collapses to 1.39 without mouth-area loss (λ=0.0) vs. 6.64 with it, indicating the core architectural claim is incomplete without explicit loss guidance

Experimental concerns: UniAvatar-Bench contains only 100 samples (too small for reliable conclusions), no statistical significance testing, no human evaluation despite claims about naturalness and quality
Unfair comparisons: Training data scales from 1.9M to 30.7M samples and model capacities vary widely (Table 6), making attribution of improvements unclear
Reproducibility barriers: No code release, vague implementation details (which keypoint detector? exact downsampling parameters?), custom dataset makes reproduction infeasible

Limited scope analysis: Evaluation focuses on talking head/speech tasks; generalization to diverse audio categories (music, ambient sounds) unclear given heavy optimization for mouth-region supervision
Two-stage training strategy (separate then joint) suggests architectural stability issues not discussed; ablation of audio initialization strategy missing
Parameter counting misleading: Reporting dual backbones (2×size) as single model capacity obscures true architectural complexity
Missing critical elements: No human listening studies, no computational cost analysis, no failure case discussion, no attention pattern visualizations

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates limitations in existing video-audio generation (lack of speech synthesis, complex fusion architectures)
Elegant architectural design: joint self-attention mechanism is simple yet effective, avoiding redundant separate attention stacks while maintaining transformer simplicity

Thorough experimental validation: comprehensive metrics across multiple dimensions (audio-video alignment, TTS quality, audio generation, video quality), strong ablations, and superior results (LSE-C=6.64, WER=0.18, PQ=6.45)
Effectively motivated mouth-area loss: well-justified by sparsity of relevant regions (~2.3% mouth, ~2.5% audio), validated through zero-masking experiments with clear visual evidence
Practical efficiency: achieves competitive performance with 3.2B parameters and 1.9M training samples vs. competitors using 7-10B params and 6-30M samples
Comprehensive dataset construction: multi-component training data with sophisticated annotation pipeline combining video captions, audio captions, and ASR
Clear presentation: well-organized structure with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1) and thorough related work contextualization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is relatively straightforward token concatenation for joint attention; primarily systems integration of existing components (Waver, MMAudio VAE, flow matching) rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Insufficient justification of design choices: initialization via parameter duplication not compared to alternatives; beyond empirics, limited insight into why joint attention fundamentally outperforms; trade-off in Table 4 (TA-RoPE improves LSE-C but degrades FD by ~19%) inadequately discussed

Reproducibility concerns: project page URL incomplete; dataset construction lacks critical details (data cleaning pipeline, availability of 700-hour talking head dataset); no code release plans mentioned; complex annotation requires tools (Tarsier2, Audio-Flamingo) that may not be readily available

Evaluation fairness issues: unequal training data amounts (JoVA 1.9M vs OVI 30.7M, Universe 1.6M) complicate baseline comparison; UniAvatar-Bench only 100 samples (potential high variance); no human evaluation (all metrics automatic); evaluation limited to human-centric talking head content

Missing analysis: no attention visualizations of learned cross-modal patterns; absence of failure case analysis; sensitivity to facial keypoint detection errors unexplored; identity consistency notably lower (0.78 vs 0.87-0.89 for audio-driven methods) without explanation; multilingual performance unknown
Computational efficiency not addressed: no discussion of inference speed, memory requirements, or computational overhead; comparison of computational efficiency vs. baselines absent

Technical clarity: Equation 4 unclear on whether text embeddings are shared or distinct; token ordering sensitivity unaddressed; batch dimension handling with different modality token counts not explained

strengths: Addresses a genuine problem: fragmented video-audio systems. Unified framework is practically valuable.
Well-designed system with elegant solutions: joint self-attention avoids disrupting pretrained priors, channel-wise conditioning solves token expansion without adding parameters.
Substantial dataset contribution: ~3M curated video-audio-text pairs with thoughtful multimodal annotation and quality filtering pipeline.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen/Edit, Verse-Bench, VBench), ablation studies validating design choices, human evaluation, strong SOTA results.
Maintains competitive video generation quality (VBench score 82.61) while adding audio generation and editing capabilities.
Clear presentation with informative figures; good implementation details provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: joint self-attention is straightforward token concatenation; joint attention via concatenation is an engineering choice rather than a methodological innovation. Should be positioned as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms paper.

Incomplete unification claim: audio-video editing limited to human-speech scenarios only; general-scene editing entirely absent. This significantly undermines the 'unified framework' claim despite being attributed to data limitations.

Synthetic data quality concerns: ~45% of dataset is synthetically generated (using FLUX, Wan2.2, etc.) for editing tasks, yet no quality analysis or comparison with real editing data. Raises questions about generalization to real-world scenarios.

Unfair experimental setup in editing task: no directly comparable baselines exist, so cascaded pipelines are constructed with ground-truth audio while JoVA jointly synthesizes audio. This makes baselines solve an easier problem and clouds the contribution of unification.

Missing critical analyses: no computational cost comparison (FLOPs, memory, inference time), no scaling analysis with dataset size, limited error analysis (only mentions of artifacts and text-preservation failures), no discussion of biases.

Significant acknowledged limitations not adequately emphasized: fast hand motion causes artifacts, text preservation fails in text-rich backgrounds, general-scene editing unsupported. These substantially limit practical applicability.
Reproducibility concerns: dataset release status unclear, code release not mentioned, quality filtering thresholds not explicitly specified, percentage of data filtered not reported.
Experimental limitations: some baseline metrics missing in tables making comprehensive comparison difficult, human evaluation limited to 50 samples, ablations primarily on one benchmark.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple metrics (LSE-C, WER, FD, KL, aesthetic scores) with diagnostic studies validating design choices
Competitive video generation quality demonstrated on VBench (total score 82.61, highest among compared methods), showing strong foundational capabilities
Well-designed system addressing practical problem of unifying video-audio generation and editing, with thoughtful data construction pipeline and honest limitation discussion
Strong performance on introduced benchmarks with diverse task coverage (generation, editing) and human subjective evaluation from 21 participants
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: joint self-attention is standard transformer concatenation of tokens; channel-wise conditioning is straightforward projection; mouth-area loss is basic masking. Core contribution is engineering integration rather than algorithmic innovation, misaligned with positioning as Algorithms/General work

Fundamentally unfair editing evaluation (Table 2): baselines receive ground-truth audio while JoVA generates both video and audio, yet paper claims superiority despite acknowledging easier baseline task. This violates fair comparison principles for a top venue

Insufficient evaluation scope: custom benchmarks too small (200 samples each for JoVABench-Gen/Edit); limited out-of-domain validation (only Verse-Bench with 600 samples); no evaluation on diverse content beyond talking heads; no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing

Synthetic data construction unvalidated: 45.2% of training data synthetically generated via FLUX.1+Wan2.2+Higgs-Audio pipeline with no analysis of artifacts, quality, or distribution shift; potential error accumulation through pipeline not discussed; no ablation comparing synthetic vs. real data

Critical scope limitations: audio-video editing explicitly limited to human-speech scenarios ('general scenes' excluded due to data scarcity); this contradicts 'unified' framing for editing capabilities

Severe reproducibility concerns: no code/model/benchmark release mentioned; no computational cost analysis (training, inference, memory); synthetic data construction details incomplete; no clear dataset access path for 3M pairs

Missing statistical rigor: Table 5 shows joint self-attention advantage is marginal (6.70 vs 6.57 LSE-C) without significance testing; human evaluation lacks variance reporting; multiple comparisons without adjustment; unfair comparison setup with baselines solving different task difficulty (ground-truth audio vs. generated)

strengths: Well-motivated unified framework addressing real fragmentation in video-audio generation and editing pipelines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks with 12+ metrics, ablation studies, and human evaluation
Strong and consistent empirical results across all benchmarks (e.g., LSE-C: 6.70 on JoVABench-Gen, best VBench score: 82.61)
Significant dataset contribution (~3M high-quality pairs) with thoughtful tri-level annotation and automated synthesis pipeline for editing
Practical design choices including channel-wise conditioning to avoid token explosion and effective mouth-area loss (1.39→6.70 LSE-C improvement)
Introduction of two new benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen, JoVABench-Edit) as community resources with careful curation and no data leakage
Clear presentation with good visual illustrations, comprehensive related work, and honest acknowledgment of limitations
Achieves state-of-the-art on pure video generation (VBench), showing unified design doesn't sacrifice individual modality quality
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: joint self-attention and channel-wise conditioning are straightforward applications of existing techniques; main contribution is their combination rather than innovation
Indirect baselines for editing comparison: cascaded pipelines (OmniVideo+Diff2Lip, Ditto+Wav2Lip) solve easier task with ground-truth audio, making architectural advantages unclear
Uneven performance across metrics: does not rank first on all evaluation dimensions (e.g., MS score on JoVABench-Edit); some improvements are incremental
Reproducibility concerns: automated dataset pipeline relies on proprietary models (GPT-4o, FLUX.1, Wan2.2, Qwen3), making independent reproduction difficult; unclear dataset/code release plans
Limited ablation studies: no justification for duplicating video parameters for audio initialization, no analysis of temporal-aligned RoPE importance, insufficient design choice validation
Code availability not mentioned, dataset release uncertain: limits reproducibility despite detailed technical descriptions
Human evaluation on modest scale: 21 participants and 50 samples per task, while reasonable, is below ideal ECCV standards for robustness
Acknowledged limitations (fast hand motion artifacts, text preservation, general-scene audio editing) mentioned but not deeply analyzed
